title: Can, may, must
title_target: ได้ ต้อง ควร — Dâai, tâwng, khuan
goal: Ask permission, say what you can do, say what you must and needn't do — and use ได้, a single word that handles three different jobs.
bekal: telling ได้, เป็น, and ไหว apart
using ต้อง (must) and ไม่ต้อง (don't need to)
asking for help with ช่วย…หน่อย

dialogs.intro: Budi asks Nok lots of questions. Watch for one word that appears eight times with three different meanings: ได้.

notes: **ได้ dâai is the most important word in this unit, and it does THREE jobs.** (1) After a verb: **can/may** — *ถ่ายรูปได้* (may take photos). (2) Alone as an answer: **"yes, sure, okay"** — *ได้ครับ*. (3) Before a verb in the form *ยังไม่ได้*: marks an action that **hasn't happened yet** (unit 11).

**Thai has THREE words for "can", and picking the wrong one sounds odd.** *ได้ dâai* = able or allowed in general. *เป็น pen* = can because you've **learned how** — for skills: *ว่ายน้ำเป็น* (can swim), *ขับรถเป็น* (can drive), *ใช้โปรแกรมนี้เป็น* (can use this program). *ไหว wǎi* = **physically able, up to it**: *เดินไหว* (can manage the walk), *กินไม่ไหว* (can't eat any more).

⚠️ **The ได้ vs เป็น difference is one of the clearest giveaways of a foreign speaker.** *ผมว่ายน้ำได้* sounds like "I'm allowed to swim"; the right way to say "I can swim" is *ผมว่ายน้ำเป็น*. Rule of thumb: if the ability has to be **learned**, use *เป็น*.

**ต้อง tâwng = must, and it goes before the verb.** *ต้องไป* (must go). Its negative isn't "mustn't" but **ไม่ต้อง mâi tâwng = don't need to**. ⚠️ A common slip: *ไม่ต้องไป* means "don't need to go", not "mustn't go". For "mustn't", use *ไปไม่ได้* or *ห้ามไป*.

**ก็ได้ kâw dâai means "that works too, whatever, fine".** *พรุ่งนี้ก็ได้* (tomorrow is fine too). It's one of the most typically Thai expressions — it signals flexibility, and you'll hear it dozens of times a day.

**ช่วย…หน่อย chûai … nàwy is the standard way to ask for help.** *ช่วยบอกหน่อย* (please tell me), *ช่วยเปิดหน่อย* (please open it). Adding *ได้ไหม* at the end makes it even softer: *ช่วยบอกหน่อยได้ไหมครับ*.
**ควร khuan = should.** Gentler than *ต้อง*, and often used for advice: *ควรจดไว้* (you should write it down). An even softer form: *น่าจะ nâa-jà* (probably should).

**รบกวนด้วยนะครับ/ค่ะ róp-kuan dûai means "sorry for the trouble".** Said after asking a favor, it's much appreciated in Thailand because it acknowledges that you've taken up someone's time. Unit 19 explains why that matters so much there.

after: ⚠️ **ห้าม hâam is the official prohibition word you see on signs**: *ห้ามสูบบุหรี่* (no smoking), *ห้ามจอด* (no parking), *ห้ามเข้า* (no entry). In everyday conversation people prefer the much gentler *…ไม่ได้*.

after: **หน่อย nàwy is a softener that's almost mandatory in every request.** Literally "a little", it shrinks the size of your request in the listener's ears. *เปิดประตูครับ* (open the door) sounds like an order; *เปิดประตูหน่อยครับ* sounds like a request.

blocks.text: Thai has a broad, subtle vocabulary of refusal, and almost all of it avoids a blunt "no". This isn't empty politeness: a direct refusal makes things awkward, and avoiding one is a sign of consideration.

blocks.title: Reading other people's refusals
items: ⚠️ If you invite someone and the answer is *ขอคิดดูก่อนนะ* or *ไว้คราวหน้านะ*, it almost always means **no**. Pushing further puts them in a tight spot, because saying no directly feels rude to them.
A rule of thumb Thai people use themselves: **if the answer isn't a clear "yes", take it as "no"** — then stop asking, kindly.

blocks.title: ถอดรองเท้า — taking off your shoes
items: This rule applies much more widely in Thailand than in most Western countries: **homes, some offices, temples, and even certain shops** expect you to take your shoes off at the door.
The cues are easy to read without any language: if there's a pile of shoes by the door, take yours off. If the floor steps up a level at the doorway, that's a sign too.

In temples, an extra rule: **never point the soles of your feet toward a Buddha image or toward people.** Sit with your legs folded back. The feet are considered the lowest part of the body and the head the highest — and that's not a metaphor but an everyday rule.
